the development of a BCI system for children and the underlying neuronal oscillations.

the SSVEP-based BCI is a promising approach for children, but the performance of children and adults differs in terms of the driving frequency and the type of stimulation.

the age-related differences in the ability to operate a stimulus-based BCI are not determined by the specific type of stimulation but by the interaction between the driving profile and the background EEG.

the age-specific performance differences in a stimulus-driven BCS are not determined by the background EEG alone but also by the type of stimulation and the underlying neuronal oscillations, which are in a functional interaction with each other.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a BCI scenario based on SSVEP should consider the development of neuronal oscillators, which are not only age specific but also frequency specific.

the ability of children to handle a SSVEP-based BCI is limited by the development of the underlying neuronal oscillator and the associated changes in the background rhythms, which in turn determine the driving profiles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SSVEP-based BCI performance is not only determined by the driving response, but also by the specific type of stimulation and the background EEG.

the age-specific differences in the SSVEP-based BCI are determined by a combination of developmental changes in the background rhythms, and the specific properties of the neuronal oscillator, driving the SSVEPs.

the SSVEP-BCI is a highly dynamic system that is influenced by age-specific changes of background activity and the respective neuronal oscillators, which is of great importance for the design and development of BCI applications.
